title: 10 Things I Hate About You
headline: 10 Things I Hate About You Is Smartest When Its Heroine Is Angriest
excerpt: A ’90s high school spin on Shakespeare that is sharpest whenever Julia Stiles' Kat gets to be furious and right at the same time.
text: Premise At a Seattle high school, new kid Cameron falls for Bianca Stratford, whose anxious dad has one rule: no dating until her older sister Kat does. Kat despises most of the school, so someone gets paid to ask her out. The Take The bones are Shakespeare’s The Taming of the Shrew, a play that treats a sharp-tongued woman as a problem to fix. This version flips the sympathy: Kat’s anger reads as intelligence, and the people irritated by her usually deserve it. What Works Everyone around Kat is a little ridiculous, on purpose: a dad who treats every date as a pregnancy scare, a guidance counselor (Allison Janney) drafting a steamy novel, and a castle-like campus scored with late-’90s guitar pop. Against that, Julia Stiles plays Kat bone-dry, so her put-downs land like verdicts. Heath Ledger plays Patrick loose and goofy; his bad-boy reputation never quite sticks. What May

title: A Quiet Place
headline: A Quiet Place Turns Every Small Sound Into a Life-or-Death Choice
excerpt: A family living in silence on a remote farm makes every creak, footstep and breath feel dangerous in this lean, 90-minute creature thriller.
text: Premise Creatures that hunt by sound have overrun the world, and the Abbott family survives on a remote farm by making almost no noise. They talk in sign language, walk barefoot on sand paths, and plan every chore around silence. The Take One rule powers this film, and John Krasinski, directing and starring opposite Emily Blunt, squeezes it until the idea of a dropped plate feels catastrophic. At 90 minutes, every scene either sets a trap or springs one, with no wasted words, partly because so few are spoken aloud. What Works The real special effect is restraint. Near-silent passages make one floorboard creak hit like a gunshot. Scenes from the perspective of the deaf daughter, Regan, played by deaf actor Millicent Simmonds, collapse into a muffled hum, and the family’s subtitled American Sign Language makes their closeness feel lived-in. title: American Murder: The Family Next Door
headline: American Murder Lets a Real Family's Own Footage Carry Their Story
excerpt: No narrator, no new interviews: this documentary rebuilds a Colorado missing-persons case from footage and messages recorded at the time.
text: Premise As the documentary presents it, the case opens in August 2018 with a call about a pregnant Colorado mother and her daughters, who cannot be reached. Every frame is something recorded before the film existed: officers’ bodycam video, phone messages and the family’s own online posts. The Take Its boldest decision is subtraction. With no narrator and no interviews filmed after the fact, nobody explains events with hindsight. Instead, the film hands you the raw record and expects you to pay close attention. What Works Shanann Watts’s own videos, full of plans, jokes and worries, keep her vivid and specific on screen instead of a name in a case file. The editing stitches timestamps, texts and doorstep footage into a timeline that tightens through small details. What May Divide Viewers That intimacy has a cost. title: Arrival
headline: Arrival Turns First Contact Into a Language Lesson With Real Suspense
excerpt: Forget laser battles: Arrival makes vocabulary the stakes, as a linguist tries to talk with visitors whose writing looks nothing like ours.
text: Premise Twelve enormous, shell-shaped craft appear around the world, and nobody knows why. The U.S. Army recruits linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) and physicist Ian Donnelly (Jeremy Renner) to communicate with the visitors before nervous governments act first. The Take Alien movies usually ask who will win. Arrival asks what a single word means, and somehow that’s tenser. Watching Louise start from one word on a whiteboard, then explain why even a simple question needs breaking down, delivers a nerdy thrill most blockbusters skip. What Works Amy Adams lets fear and curiosity flicker across her face instead of spilling into speeches. Bradford Young’s camera soaks everything in fog and overcast light, so the visitors feel truly foreign. Jóhann Jóhannsson’s score hums with layered voices that sound almost like breathing, and the visitors’ circular, inky script is wonderfully strange. title: Crazy Rich Asians
headline: Crazy Rich Asians Is a Glossy Fairy Tale With a Sharp Family Standoff Inside
excerpt: A lavish Singapore rom-com whose best scenes are Constance Wu and Michelle Yeoh sizing each other up across the family table.
text: Premise Rachel Chu, a New York economics professor, flies to Singapore with boyfriend Nick for his best friend’s wedding. Nick never mentioned that his family is staggeringly rich, or that not everyone will welcome her. The Take Nick is charming, yet he’s the least interesting person here. The real story is Rachel decoding a world that has already judged her, led by Nick’s icy mother, Eleanor. Jon M. Chu stages a fairy tale, then lets class tension slice through the sparkle. What Works Every surface signals rank. Costumes mark who belongs, a feast at a hawker center (an open-air food court) sells Singapore better than any skyline, and the soundtrack swaps in Chinese-language covers of English pop hits. Amid the gloss, Michelle Yeoh barely raises her voice, and Eleanor is scarier for it; the script gives her reasons, not villainy. title: Get Out
headline: Get Out Finds the Horror Hiding Inside a Polite Weekend Visit
excerpt: Jordan Peele turns a meet-the-parents weekend into creeping social horror, where every friendly smile feels like a test.
text: Premise Chris, a young Black photographer, spends a weekend with his white girlfriend Rose’s parents at their secluded country home. Their welcome is almost aggressively warm, but the staff, the guests and the small talk keep feeling off. The Take Jordan Peele gets that plenty of real-life fear is social: the compliment that lands wrong, the host who insists once too often that he’s open-minded. Get Out turns those tiny humiliations into a thriller’s engine, and for long stretches its scariest set piece is a backyard party. What Works Daniel Kaluuya plays Chris as someone constantly editing his reactions, and tight close-ups let you watch him swallow every awkward exchange. Lil Rel Howery, as best friend Rod, gets the big laughs while voicing what viewers are already thinking. Michael Abels’s choral score sounds like a warning nobody on screen can hear. title: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone
headline: Sorcerer's Stone Is a Tour of Hogwarts First and a Mystery Second
excerpt: Less a tight mystery than a guided tour of a magic school, with a stacked adult cast and sets that do much of the storytelling.
text: Premise Harry Potter has spent most of his childhood sleeping in a cupboard under his relatives’ stairs. Then mysterious letters arrive, a giant of a groundskeeper turns up, and Harry learns he’s a wizard with a place at Hogwarts. The Take Sorcerer’s Stone works like a guided tour with a mystery tucked in its back pocket. Chris Columbus gives most of the runtime to showing Harry (and you) around, from moving staircases to broomstick sport, before the plot finally takes the wheel. As storytelling, that’s lopsided. As a first visit to a world, it’s generous. What Works The sets carry much of the storytelling: Diagon Alley feels crammed and lived-in, and the Great Hall’s floating candles sell wonder without dialogue. John Williams’s twinkly main theme sets the mood within seconds. The grown-up cast is stacked, from Maggie Smith’s crisp McGonagall to Alan Rickman’s slow-burn sneer. What May Divide Viewers The

title: Hereditary
headline: Hereditary Treats Family Grief as the Scariest Thing in the House
excerpt: Toni Collette anchors a slow, punishing horror film about a family coming apart after a funeral, with unease that seeps in rather than jumps out.
text: Premise After her guarded, difficult mother dies, miniature artist Annie Graham (Toni Collette) tries to hold her household together while untangling her mixed feelings about her. Grief makes everyone stranger, and small, unexplained things start piling up. The Take Think of this as a family tragedy that happens to be terrifying. Ari Aster lets old resentments and everything this family won’t say out loud do most of the haunting, so the uncanny seems to grow out of damage already there. It’s the bleakest film in our horror lineup, on purpose. What Works Collette is ferocious, swinging from brittle politeness to anguish that’s hard to watch. The opening shot pushes into one of Annie’s model rooms until it becomes real, and the camera keeps framing the family like diorama figures. Colin Stetson’s low, wheezing score simmers underneath like a fever. What May Divide Viewers The first hour moves at the speed

title: How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days
headline: How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days Plays Romance Like a Rigged Card Game
excerpt: Two schemers, one ten-day deadline: Kate Hudson and Matthew McConaughey turn a double con into a sparring match.
text: Premise Magazine columnist Andie wants to write serious stories, but her next article requires dating a man and driving him off within ten days. Ad executive Ben bets he can make a woman fall for him in that same window. They end up dating each other, both hiding an agenda. The Take The double con is a clever engine. Because you know both secrets, every date plays like a duel: each clingy stunt from Andie is an attack, and each time Ben swallows it, he’s protecting his wager. What Works Kate Hudson commits to being exhausting, down to a “love fern” she insists they share, and never winks to apologize. Matthew McConaughey plays the straight man, his grin cracking a little more with each test. The best stretch is a weekend with Ben’s family on Staten Island, where a rowdy card game loosens everyone up. What May Divide Viewers Andie’s

title: Howl's Moving Castle
headline: Howl's Moving Castle Runs on Mood, and Mostly Gets Away With It
excerpt: A tangled plot rides on gorgeous design: a wheezing walking castle, a blunt heroine and a waltz that makes housework feel romantic.
text: Premise Sophie is a quiet young hatmaker in a town bracing for war. When a spiteful witch curses her into the body of an old woman, she strikes out alone and lets herself into the walking castle of Howl, a wizard with an alarming reputation. The Take Next to Spirited Away, the story is looser and more knotted, but the film cares more about feelings than mechanics: being underestimated, making a home out of a mess, falling for someone flighty. On those terms, it mostly earns its two hours. What Works The castle is wonderfully odd: a clanking heap of turrets and chimneys on spindly bird legs, wheezing as it lurches along. Sophie is a practical, plainspoken lead who fixes problems with a broom rather than a spell. Calcifer, the grumpy fire demon powering it all, gets the best laughs. title: Inception
headline: Inception Makes the Rulebook the Most Exciting Part of the Heist
excerpt: Christopher Nolan hands you a dream-heist rulebook in the first hour, then spends the second hour testing every rule at once.
text: Premise Dom Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio) steals secrets by slipping into people’s dreams. A powerful client offers him a way home, but the job flips his usual work: instead of taking an idea out of someone’s head, his crew has to plant one. The Take Inception’s smartest move is handing you the instruction manual up front. Every rule you learn early, about falling, time and layers, becomes a ticking clock later, so the tension comes from knowing what could break. What Works The crew plays like a real team: Joseph Gordon-Levitt as the precise planner, Tom Hardy as the smirking improviser, Elliot Page as the newcomer asking your questions. Several set pieces were built for real, including a hallway that actually rotates, and Hans Zimmer’s foghorn-like brass makes whole scenes feel tilted. title: Interstellar
headline: Interstellar Is a Family Drama in a Spacesuit, and That's Its Strength
excerpt: The science talk gets heavy, but Interstellar's real engine is a father's promise to his kids, carried by a roaring pipe-organ score.
text: Premise Dust storms and failing crops are choking a near-future Earth, and ex-pilot Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) now farms corn and raises two kids. A secret mission through a wormhole might find humanity a new home, but joining means leaving his family. The Take Let’s be upfront: Interstellar is long, earnest and sometimes clunky. It lands anyway, because beneath the black holes it’s about the cost of leaving: every choice in space is weighed against the people waiting at the farmhouse. What Works Hans Zimmer built the score around a church pipe organ, so deep space sounds sacred and lonely at once. Outside the ship, sound often drops to near silence, a bold contrast with the roar of launch. McConaughey’s weathered warmth anchors everything, while TARS, a boxy robot with an adjustable humor setting, steals scenes. title: Spirited Away
headline: Spirited Away Makes Growing Up Look Like Learning a New Job
excerpt: Miyazaki swaps swords for scrub brushes, building a coming-of-age fantasy out of chores, courtesy and quiet nerve.
text: Premise Ten-year-old Chihiro is sulking in the back seat when her parents take a wrong turn into what looks like an abandoned theme park. By nightfall it’s crowded with spirits, her parents are in serious trouble, and she must find work at a bathhouse for the gods. The Take Most fantasy heroes get a sword. Chihiro gets a scrub brush. Hayao Miyazaki builds the film around labor, manners and small acts of nerve, which is why it feels so unlike Western quest stories. She grows up by showing up for shifts and keeping her word. What Works The bathhouse is drawn like a real workplace, with a boiler room, steam and shared staff sleeping quarters, so the magic feels grounded. Joe Hisaishi’s gentle, piano-led themes leave room for quiet, and a nearly wordless train ride lands harder than any chase. Chihiro’s slouchy, whiny body language early on is unusually honest

title: The Conjuring
headline: The Conjuring Builds Its Scares the Old-Fashioned Way, and It Works
excerpt: Gliding camerawork, 1970s textures and a sincere investigator couple turn this haunted-farmhouse story into chills that build room by room.
text: Premise In 1971, the Perron family moves into a rambling Rhode Island farmhouse, and trouble starts fast: stopped clocks, a foul smell, unexplained bruises. They call Ed and Lorraine Warren, married paranormal investigators played by Patrick Wilson and Vera Farmiga. The Take There’s no wink here. James Wan plays this ghost story straight, betting on suspense over blood, and that earnestness is why it works: each fright hits people you’ve started to care about. What Works Watch the camera. Long, unbroken moves through hallways and stairwells map the house, so you always know where the dark corners are, which makes them worse. A family game of hide-and-clap becomes the film’s best scare, built from little more than darkness and sound. Lili Taylor, as the Perron mother, supplies raw nerve, while wood paneling and period clothes sell the era. What May Divide Viewers The ingredients are familiar: creaking doors, a music

title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring
headline: The Fellowship of the Ring Makes Every Mile of Its Long Walk Count
excerpt: Peter Jackson turns sheer distance into the spectacle, and Howard Shore's music makes leaving the Shire ache.
text: Premise Frodo Baggins likes his quiet life in the Shire, until his eccentric relative Bilbo leaves him a ring with a terrible history. It turns out a dark lord needs that ring to conquer Middle-earth, so Frodo has to carry it far from home. The Take This is a movie about walking, and it knows it. Peter Jackson makes distance itself the main event: every ridge the hobbits cross pulls them farther from comfort. The battles are big, but the real tension is whether ordinary people can keep going. What Works Howard Shore’s score gives places their own melodies, so a few bars of the Shire’s folksy tune later carry a pang of homesickness. Forced perspective (placing actors at different distances from the camera) still makes hobbits look convincingly tiny beside wizards. title: The Hatchet Wielding Hitchhiker
headline: The Hatchet Wielding Hitchhiker Asks What Happens After the Internet Laughs
excerpt: A viral 2013 news clip gets a second look in a documentary more interested in internet attention than in the meme itself.
text: Premise The documentary revisits 2013, when a hitchhiker known as Kai gives a wildly quotable interview to a Fresno, California, TV station about a roadside attack he says he stopped. As the clip races across the internet, the film retraces that moment through news footage and people who met him. The Take The real subject is the audience. The film reminds you how fun the clip felt, then quietly asks what it means to turn a frightening real event, and the stranger caught up in it, into a catchphrase. What Works Early stretches bounce along on remixes, talk-show buzz and meme montages, then the mood cools gradually instead of flipping a switch. Voices from his offline life add a texture the original clip never had. title: The Matrix
headline: In The Matrix, the Style Does the Explaining
excerpt: Leather coats, green-tinted screens and slow-motion gunfights aren't decoration in The Matrix; they teach you how its world works.
text: Premise By day, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) works in a cubicle; by night, he’s a hacker called Neo, chasing rumors about the Matrix. Then the mysterious Morpheus (Laurence Fishburne) and Trinity (Carrie-Anne Moss) offer him answers, at a price. The Take This could have been a lecture about reality wearing sunglasses. Instead, every visual choice carries an idea. The chunky 1999 monitors look dated, but the logic holds: learn this world’s rules and each fight becomes an argument about what a person can do. What Works Color does quiet storytelling: scenes inside the Matrix carry a sickly green tint that makes even offices feel subtly wrong. Yuen Woo-ping’s choreography gives the kung fu real snap, and “bullet time” freezes moments while the camera swoops around them. Hugo Weaving plays Agent Smith with a clipped, contemptuous calm. title: The Proposal
headline: The Proposal Puts a Control Freak at the Mercy of Small-Town Alaska
excerpt: A boss fakes an engagement to her assistant, and Sandra Bullock and Ryan Reynolds' prickly back-and-forth carries it all the way to Alaska.
text: Premise Feared Manhattan book editor Margaret Tate is Canadian, and a visa mess could get her deported. Her fix: announce an engagement to her overworked assistant, Andrew, which means a weekend at his family’s home in Sitka, Alaska. The Take Watching someone who controls every room lose control of all of them is the whole joke, and a good one. At the office, Margaret holds the leash. Up north, Andrew’s family, his hometown and even the local wildlife take it. What Works Andrew’s family earns as many laughs as the leads. Betty White, as his grandmother, gets the strangest, funniest material, and the sunny harbor town makes the Paxtons feel lived-in. Dropped into that, Sandra Bullock commits to every humiliation, including one mortifying collision, while Ryan Reynolds answers so dryly that their insults bounce instead of sting. What May Divide Viewers The first half zips along on quick put-downs. Once

title: The Tinder Swindler
headline: The Tinder Swindler Shows How a Jet-Set Fantasy Gets Sold One Text at a Time
excerpt: Rom-com gloss and real text threads let the women at its center show how, as they tell it, a jet-set dating fantasy became a money trap.
text: Premise Several women describe meeting a charming, seemingly ultra-rich man on Tinder. The film traces how those relationships moved from private jets to urgent pleas for cash, using their saved messages, voice notes and photos. The Take Starting out as a dating-app fairy tale is the film’s smartest move. You feel the lifestyle’s pull before any red flags appear, so the smug “how could anyone fall for this” reaction is hard to keep. It is persuasion, shown from the inside. What Works The interviewees are sharp and funny, and the film treats them as people with evidence, not punchlines. Texts pop up on screen as if arriving live, making the pressure feel uncomfortably immediate. What May Divide Viewers The polish is both the hook and the problem. Travel-ad visuals and staged recreations make it addictive, but risk turning the debt and heartbreak the women describe into a breezy caper. The

title: What Jennifer Did
headline: What Jennifer Did Turns a Police Interview Room Into the Whole Story
excerpt: Built around police interview tapes, this documentary turns a 2010 Ontario home-invasion case into a tense, slow-burn procedural.
text: Premise According to the film, in 2010 a young woman called emergency services to report an armed break-in at her family’s home in Markham, Ontario. It follows the detectives on the case through their recorded interviews with her. The Take Most of the tension lives in one plain interview room. Built on police footage, the film turns pauses, follow-up questions and long silences into the main events. Gripping, yes, but told largely from the investigators’ side of the table. What Works The pacing is patient. Clips run long enough for you to form your own read before an interviewee weighs in, and at under 90 minutes it never drifts. title: Don't Say Good Luck
headline: Don't Say Good Luck Finds the Laughs Backstage While Life Gets Heavy at Home
excerpt: A theater kid lands the lead in her school's Waitress as her mom's cancer returns, in a gentle, funny drama that refuses to become a weepie.
text: Premise Sixteen-year-old Sophie Birenbaum (Sunny Sandler) is chasing the lead in her high school’s production of Waitress just as her mother, Elizabeth (Melanie Lynskey), learns her cancer is back. Her parents want to keep the news quiet, so Sophie ends up juggling rehearsals, a crush on her scene partner and a family trying very hard to act normal. The Take This could have been a disease-of-the-week weepie. Instead, director Julia Hart and co-writer Laura Hankin, who drew on her own high school years, make a theater-kid movie that happens to have something devastating at its center. It’s about living alongside bad news rather than counting down to it, and that restraint is its smartest choice. The title nods to the stage superstition that wishing an actor “good luck” jinxes the show, and the whole film runs on that same nervous mix of hope and dread. What Works Lynskey is the

title: Hocus Pocus
headline: Hocus Pocus Is Messy, Silly and Saved by Three Perfect Witches
excerpt: Bette Midler, Sarah Jessica Parker and Kathy Najimy turn a lumpy kids' adventure into the Halloween rewatch nobody outgrows.
text: Premise In 1693 Salem, the three Sanderson sisters are hanged for witchcraft, and a boy who tried to stop them is cursed to live forever as a black cat. Three hundred years later, new kid Max (Omri Katz) takes his little sister Dani (Thora Birch) trick-or-treating, scoffs at the local legend and accidentally brings the witches back for one very long Halloween night. The Take Hocus Pocus is two movies stitched together, and only one of them is good. The kids-on-an-adventure half is thin. The witches half is a gleeful, scenery-chewing comedy, and it’s the reason a 1993 box-office disappointment turned into an October ritual. Every time Bette Midler, Sarah Jessica Parker and Kathy Najimy share the frame, the movie comes alive. title: Five Genres, Five Starting Points: What Should You Watch Tonight?
headline: Five Genres, Five Starting Points: What Should You Watch Tonight?
excerpt: New to sci-fi, true crime, fantasy, rom-coms or horror? Here is one easy way in for each genre, and the kind of night each pick gives you.
text: Trying a genre you don’t usually watch can feel like a gamble. Pick the wrong first title and you might write off the whole category. Here’s one starting point for each of our five launch genres: why it works as a way in, what kind of night it gives you, and how it compares with the other four, so you can choose tonight. Sci-Fi: Inception Inception is one big sci-fi idea with a heist movie built around it. Leonardo DiCaprio plays a thief who steals secrets from people’s dreams, hired for a job that flips the usual task: plant an idea instead of taking one. Why it’s a good door: no spaceships or genre knowledge required. The film explains its own rules, then has fun bending them, and shows that sci-fi can be about how your mind works. title: Welcome to Twisted Takes
headline: Welcome to Twisted Takes
excerpt: Who we are, why a group of students started a movie and TV review community, and how you can join the conversation.
text: Twisted Takes is a movie and TV review community run by a team of students. You can also find us on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, where we keep things quick. This blog is where we slow down: longer reviews, recommendations and questions worth arguing about. Why we started We share an interest in entertainment and, honestly, in the conversations it creates. Some of the best parts of watching something happen after the credits, when you find out a friend saw a completely different movie than you did. We want to help people decide what to watch next and give them a place to compare opinions, not just collect them. Why “Twisted”? Because a take gets more interesting when it bends a little. “Twisted” stands for different perspectives on the same title, and for recommendations you might not expect, like a horror pick for someone who swears they only watch rom-coms.

title: Fantasy Worlds Worth Getting Lost In
headline: Fantasy Worlds Worth Getting Lost In
excerpt: Middle-earth, Hogwarts, a spirit bathhouse and a walking castle: four fantasy worlds, matched to the kind of night you actually want.
text: Fantasy is one of the few genres where the setting can matter as much as the story. You don’t just watch these movies. You hang out in them for a few hours, and the place itself sets the mood. That’s why choosing between them has less to do with which one is “best” and more to do with what kind of evening you’re after. Three of these four came out in 2001, yet they could hardly feel more different to spend time in. Here’s how we’d match each one to a mood. The Fellowship of the Ring: the epic weekend commitment The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring is the one you plan for. It runs close to three hours, it’s the opening chapter of a much longer story, and it asks you to care about maps, old histories and a lot of walking. That’s the appeal.

title: If You Liked Inception, Watch These Next
headline: If You Liked Inception, Watch These Next
excerpt: Three follow-ups for Inception fans, each pulling a different thread: bigger feelings, a quieter puzzle, or reality-bending action.
text: Inception is technically a heist movie, but the heist is rarely what people come back for. If it stuck with you, you’re probably chasing a few things at once: rules you pick up on the fly, a story that trusts you to keep up, big practical spectacle, and a personal ache sitting under all the clever machinery. No single movie hits every one of those. So instead of three copies, here are three films that each pull on a different thread. Pick the one that matches the part you liked most. Interstellar: for the emotional scale Interstellar comes from the same director, Christopher Nolan, and you’ll recognize the instincts: enormous sets, a booming Hans Zimmer score, and a plot that treats time as something that can stretch. title: Pick Your Next Movie by Mood
headline: Pick Your Next Movie by Mood
excerpt: Not sure what to watch? Start with how you feel. Thirteen launch titles sorted into five moods, from thoughtful to properly unsettling.
text: Genre tells you what a movie is. Mood tells you whether it’s right for tonight. A horror film and a documentary can scratch the same itch, while two romantic comedies can feel nothing alike. So here’s a different way into our launch catalog: figure out how you feel, then pick from the list. Every title links to its full spoiler-free review if you want more before you press play. Thoughtful For when you want something to chew on after the credits. Arrival is a first-contact movie where the big set piece is a conversation. It’s patient and quiet, and it leaves you wondering what it really takes to understand someone. Get Out is horror that works as social satire. Jordan Peele puts its sharpest moments in awkward small talk, not jump scares, so expect to want to talk it through afterward. The Tinder Swindler lets the women at its center
